One pipeline, two guarantees

100 seed problems, every one carrying a proof that compiles here and a three-rung hint ladder. From those, mutation and crossover breed a corpus; every child passes the same gates its parents did.

100seeds, both benchmarks
100proofs verified in a fresh process
100axiom closures clean
50also reproducible on 2 platforms

The seeds are a selection, not an inheritance — how they were chosen, and every one of them, is on its own page. What follows is what happens to them.

Every seed already carries a proof, so the Gen-0 branch below is idle today. It stays because the branch is a property of the pipeline, not of a benchmark: a seed arrives with a proof or it does not, and where it came from stops mattering once it has passed the gates. Labelling that branch ProofNet and miniF2F described one loading of the corpus, not the architecture.

The validation layer is where most of the work is. It runs six gates in order — the statement must elaborate, mean what the prose says, be proved, rest only on permitted axioms, replay through an independent kernel, and export identically on a second platform — and a candidate keeps whichever level it reached rather than being discarded at the first refusal. The syntactic gates and the ladder they produce are on Certification; the one that asks whether the Lean says what the problem says is on Faithfulness, because type checking cannot answer it and it is the harder question.

What runs it

The pipeline is two LangGraph state machines, and every stage inside them reports to LangSmith. Neither is decoration: the fan-out below is why a generation is a graph rather than a loop, and the tracing is how the failures on this site were found at all.

flowchart TB
  subgraph OUT["Pool graph — one run per generation"]
    A1["01 load_seed_pool"] --> A2["02 orchestrator_plan_generation"]
    A2 --> A3["03 slot_dispatch"]
    A3 -->|"Send() per slot"| A4["04 slot_unit"]
    A4 --> A5["05 slot_aggregate"]
    A5 --> A6["06 save_generation"]
    A6 -->|"next generation"| A2
  end
  A4 --> B1
  subgraph INN["Certification graph — one run per candidate"]
    B1["generate_candidate"] --> B2["detect_family"]
    B2 --> B3["template"]
    B3 --> B4["anti_stub"]
    B4 --> B5["lean_health"]
    B5 --> B6["lean_check"]
    B4 -->|"retry"| B1
    B5 -->|"retry"| B3
  end
  classDef n fill:#e2f0ef,stroke:#0E7C7B,color:#12312f
  class A1,A2,A3,A4,A5,A6,B1,B2,B3,B4,B5,B6 n

LangGraph · why a graph

A generation is not a sequence of candidates but a fan-out: slot_dispatch issues one Send per slot, each slot runs the whole certification graph independently, and slot_aggregate is the barrier that decides whether another generation follows.

Conditional edges carry the retries. A candidate that fails anti_stub returns to generation with the diagnostic attached rather than being discarded — the retry is an edge in the graph, so it is bounded and recorded instead of being a loop someone has to remember to cap.

LangSmith · why it earned its place

29 trace points, nested to the turn: a seed run opens a span, each attempt and each turn nests inside it, and the model call and the Lean verdict sit side by side at the leaf.

That granularity is what surfaced the leak on this project. A proof run looked merely slow; the traces showed 8 of 29 model calls returning zero characters with codex exec exited with code 1 — the CLI crashing — while each still consumed a turn of the budget. No aggregate metric would have separated that from a hard problem.

The seed set

100 problems, chosen rather than inherited. Both source benchmarks are larger; what made a problem a seed was passing every gate we could run on it, not being in the release.

ProofNet-Verified · 50

miniF2F-v2 · 50

Topic shares track each corpus rather than a flat draw, so the set stays a scale model of what it came from. Difficulty is split at each corpus's own tertiles of proof length — 34 easy / 34 medium / 32 hard overall — which means “hard” names a different thing in each, and analysis has to say which.

Why the top level had to change

The old top level was called replay_certified, and it stopped at the comparator. That check is real — it replays the exported term through a kernel Lean's elaborator did not write — but it still runs in exactly one environment: ours. It cannot answer the question that matters to whoever downloads the release.

We know the size of that gap because we measured it on the benchmark we inherited. ProofNet-Verified ships as verified. Under our pin, a quarter of it does not compile.

replays under our pin
272
other
47
signature drift
18
unsolved goals
15
unknown identifier
15

367 released rows, lean4:v4.30.0-rc2 · Mathlib 0fb20450. Their authors were not wrong — their check was local, and nothing in the artifact said what “local” meant. Publishing our own corpus the same way would repeat it.

This number was wrong once, and the correction is the point.

The first measurement said 249/367 — 32% failing. Asked for examples, we found the missing identifiers were not Mathlib's at all: odd_pow_plus_one_dvd, contractionConstant, Landau175.sup_nonneg_of_bdd. They were helper lemmas the ground-truth files declare between their theorems, and our header extraction stopped at the first declaration. We had blamed a released benchmark for a file we assembled badly.

Rebuilding the context — slicing the problem's own theorems out of the ground-truth file and keeping everything else, so namespace structure and helper ordering survive — recovered 23 rows and cut unknown identifier from 48 to 15. The remaining 95 are dominated by ambiguity and signature changes (Prime resolving to both _root_.Prime and Nat.Prime, IsMulCommutative.comm gone), which look like drift — but we have not finished separating those from our own open set, so 26% is an upper bound on drift, not a measurement of it.

What makes the stronger claim checkable

lean4export is deterministic across operating systems. Same toolchain, same package revisions, byte-identical term:

macOS · aarch64

0558270ede426ac1f7c9cc90… 34,392,833 bytes

Linux · aarch64

0558270ede426ac1f7c9cc90… 34,392,833 bytes

So one hash certifies the whole environment. A third party who matches our published pins regenerates the export and compares a single digest — no access to our machine, our elaborator, or the 1.5 GB of terms. We publish the digests and the recipe rather than the terms themselves.

Two traps, both hit on the first attempt. The export must be produced by the same recipe everywhere: run inside a Lake project instead of plain lean + LEAN_PATH and a different set of modules enters the environment, changing the term's dependency closure — 34 MB against 20 MB, indistinguishable from real nondeterminism. And the working directory needs its own lean-toolchain, or elan silently resolves the machine default; the host picked a different Lean and rejected our oleans outright. A reproducibility check that leans on an unpinned default has no business granting the level.

What a certificate now records

Mathlib's revision alone under-described the pin by nine packages — a proof breaks on a batteries or aesop bump just as readily. Every certificate now carries all ten plus a digest over them:

toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2 package_revisions Cli · LeanSearchClient · Qq · aesop · batteries importGraph · mathlib · plausible · proofwidgets · repl manifest_digest 262dfbd6193e7c04 platforms_verified macos-aarch64 · linux-aarch64

The upgrade to reproducible refuses fewer than two distinct platforms — one machine agreeing with itself is the failure mode being guarded, so it raises rather than passing with a caveat. It also requires kernel_replayed underneath: reproducing a weaker check more widely is more evidence of the same kind, not evidence of a stronger kind.

Where miniF2F stops, and why

miniF2F withholds its proofs on purpose — the maintainers decline proof contributions to keep the test set uncontaminated — so no ground truth exists to replay. Gen-0 generates the only proof there is, which puts those seeds at proof_checked by construction. Same ladder, different reachable ceiling, and the certificate column says which so the two never blur.

50/50seeds proved and re-verified
8of the original draw replaced
13/16spares proved, 8 taken
81%spare proof rate

Eight of the first fifty did not survive, and the reasons split cleanly. Five were rejected by the faithfulness gate even after doubling the proof budget — amc12_2000_p1 asks for distinct I, M, O but its Lean carries only I ≠ M ∧ M ≠ O, admitting I = O. Two exhausted the per-seed clock. One never reached a proof attempt at all.

That one is mathd_algebra_275, which writes (11 : ℝ) ^ (1 / 4) — 1/4 elaborates as natural division and collapses to 0, so the hypothesis says 1 = 1/5, every goal follows, and norm_num at h “proves” the theorem without touching the mathematics. A vacuity screen now asks Lean whether False follows from the hypotheses alone before any budget is spent. Replacements are drawn from the family currently most under-filled, not in file order: the families needing a top-up are the ones whose seeds were hardest to prove, so first-come order would have tilted the set toward easy problems.

Faithfulness

The trusted object is not the statement string — it is the goal Lean elaborated from it. Three roles, separated by what each one is allowed to see. This is the goal_roundtrip gate: the one check type checking cannot decide, and one of eleven the validation layer runs. The rest are below.

The whole validation layer

A generated theorem can be sound Lean and still be worthless. It can be true because nothing satisfies its hypotheses; it can be a statement the corpus already contains; it can be a corollary its parent's proof already discharges; and it can prove something other than the problem it is released as. None of those is visible to a type checker, and no two are the same kind of question — so each check sits with the faculty that can settle the one it asks.

  • Determinate questions go to Lean. Whether a statement elaborates, whether a proof closes, which axioms it rests on, whether the hypotheses can hold at once, whether each one is load-bearing. Each is a compilation whose outcome is the verdict.
  • Identity goes to a hash. Whether two rows state the same theorem is not a matter of degree, so it is not a matter for a judge. Statements are compared under an alpha-normal form, against every earlier campaign rather than the current run.
  • Meaning goes to a reader, twice. Whether a child demands reasoning its parent does not supply, and whether the prose describes the theorem underneath, are questions of degree. One verdict is evidence; admission needs two.
  • Independence goes to a kernel that did not produce the proof. The comparator rebuilds the statement from the trusted row alone and replays the term. It is the one check whose value comes from not being ours.
CheckDecided byWhat it settlesCoverage
statement_type_checkLeanthe statement is well-formed Lean and invents nothing535/535
proof_acceptedLeanthe proof closes, with no sorry535/535
axiom_auditLeanthe proof rests on Lean's standard axioms and nothing else535/535
vacuityLeanthe hypotheses can all hold at once, so the theorem is not free535/535
dead_hypothesesLeanevery hypothesis is load-bearing535/535
corpus_deduphashthe statement is not already in the corpus under another name535/535
redundancyLeanno hypothesis can be deleted, no parent proves itself518/518 applicable
hypothesis_preservationparsera silent mutation kept every hypothesis its parent had (silent only)16/17 applicable
comparatorLeanan independent runner replays the proof through the kernel535/535
goal_roundtripmodelthe elaborated goal is the problem the prose states535/535

Two checks are reported over the rows they apply to, so a blank reads as inapplicability rather than as a gap: a hypothesis comparison means nothing where the operator was not asked to preserve them, and a silent mutation is equivalent to its parent by design, so asking whether it adds anything would report the operator working.

Redundancy is asked by deleting, never by adding. A hypothesis is removed from the child and a prover is asked to close the goal without it; a parent is stripped of every hypothesis and offered alone. Deleting makes the statement strictly harder, so Lean closing it afterwards has only one explanation. Asked the other way round — handing the prover the parent as an extra hypothesis — the question cannot fail: the child's own proof closes it with the parent unused. That form ran once over the whole release, reported 66 of 165 rows redundant, and a control substituting a hypothesis with no mathematics in it reproduced four of the first six findings. It was removed.

Why this set suffices

A released row can be wrong in four ways, and the layer covers all four.

The row is…Excluded by
not a theoremstatement_type_check, proof_accepted, axiom_audit — and re-established independently by comparator
a theorem for a degenerate reasonvacuity, dead_hypotheses
a theorem the corpus already has, or one that assumes more than it usescorpus_dedup, redundancy
a fine theorem released as a different problemgoal_roundtrip

The redundancy probe and the round-trip decide against the judge rather than after it. Of the 171 candidates two independent judge passes both rated strong and voted to keep, the round-trip removed 12 for stating a problem other than the one Lean elaborated and held back 1 more whose verdict it never returned, and the redundancy probe removed a further 11 for holding a hypothesis Lean could delete. 147 remain. These gates run last and get the final word because each carries a proof where the judge carries an opinion — and because a standard that bends for a well-written problem is not a standard.

Admission reads both halves of each judgement, and it did not always. A judge returns a quality and a vote, and they answer different questions: how good the problem is, and whether it belongs in the corpus at all. Reading only the first admitted six rows the judge had voted to reject — two of them rejected by both passes — every one for recall, the label for a problem that is good and already covered by a sibling. Those are exactly the rows the second question exists to catch.

That is a claim about coverage of failure kinds, not about detection rates, and it is made in that form deliberately. Three of these checks are one-sided: a redundancy probe that finds no proof has found nothing, and the same is true of vacuity and of the judge's uncertainty. Where a check cannot fail on the thing it exists to catch it does not belong here at all — two were removed on exactly that ground, and a third for the sharper reason that it could not fail at all. What remains is the set for which we can say, of each member, both what it decides and what its silence does not mean.

Four checks changed what they are

Each of these was trusted before it was measured. What follows is what each one claimed, what it does now, and the measurement that forced the change.

redundancy

added the parent as a hypothesis → deletes a hypothesis and re-proves

The old form asked a prover to close (hP : parent) (child binders) : child goal. Every certified child makes that true with hP unused, so it was provable for the whole corpus: run over the release it called 66 of 165 rows redundant, and a control putting a contentless hypothesis in the parent's place reproduced four of the first six. It measured prover strength. What replaced it deletes a hypothesis instead, which makes the statement strictly harder, and it is now a gate rather than a note — 12 rows two judge passes both called strong were dropped by it.

silent_equivalence

decided the row → informs the judge

Asked to derive parent and child from each other. Both are theorems, so a direction closes whether or not the hypothesis is used: tested directly it passed a child that had dropped a conjunct, and an unrelated true statement. It could not fail on the cases it existed to catch.

dead_hypotheses

searched the proof for the name → removes it and recompiles

The name search was right 24 times out of 53, because omega, simp_all and linarith consume hypotheses without naming one. Lean deciding it found 25 genuinely dead hypotheses across 14 released rows, repeated to a fixpoint because removing one can make another dead.

corpus_dedup

blanked binder declarations → alpha-normalises the statement

Binder names were erased where they were declared and left where they were used, so the same closure identity over n and over r hashed differently. Four alpha-equivalent pairs had been released.

What is still not settled

  • Kernel replay. 0 of 535 workspaces are built and none has been replayed (535/535). Comparator's sandbox is Landlock, so it runs on Linux and this corpus was assembled on macOS. Every row sits at proof_checked; none claims kernel_replayed.
  • Round-trip coverage. The gate diagrammed above ran on 535 of 535 released rows. The numbers below it are from the benchmark that validated the gate, not from this corpus.
  • The judge disagrees with itself. Run twice over the same 1233 rows in the same order, it agreed on keep-or-reject 79% of the time. That is the ceiling on any single verdict, and it is why release admission needs two.

Exam environment

The certified statement is the exam’s starting state. Play a tactic, watch the goal state change — this is the real loop, driven by a recorded episode.

    Four real episodes, replayed. The goal states are what Lean produced when these proofs were checked — scripts/export_exam_demo.py re-ran each recorded run through the environment to capture them. Only the tactic the episode actually played advances the state; anything else is rejected, which is also how the live environment behaves.

    The three hints, and what each is for

    Help is offered in three kinds, not three doses. Each answers a different question a stuck solver might be asking, and every one of the 100 seeds carries all three.

    1 · lemma names

    FiniteField.prod_univ_units_id_eq_neg_one

    For the solver who knows the mathematics but cannot find the name. Drawn from the proof; where a proof cites nothing, from the concepts the statement is about.

    2 · outline

    The nonzero elements form a cyclic group, in which every element pairs with its inverse except those equal to their own inverse.

    Strategy in prose. Naming a tactic here would make this rung a weaker copy of the next one, so a lint rejects outlines that do — it caught three of our own while they were being written.

    3 · first step

    have h : (∏ x : Kˣ, x) = (-1 : Kˣ) :=

    One concrete line. This is the only rung that gives away part of the answer, and it is flagged as such.

    Two ways the ladder collapses

    Measuring it rather than assuming it turned up two failures, one of which we fixed and one we could only record.

    Fixed · the first line was rarely the first idea

    Taking the literal opening line made level 3 read classical or revert n hn — entering classical logic, moving binders. That costs the solver a rung and says nothing.

    before · bookkeeping
    54
    after · a real step
    100

    Level 3 now skips tactics that rearrange the proof state without deciding anything, and returns the first line that commits to an idea. 54 of 100 rows changed; none still open on bookkeeping.

    Recorded · sometimes rung 1 outranks rung 2

    Where a proof is one application of one lemma, naming that lemma is the proof — so the weakest rung is the strongest. A one-line proof cannot be hinted at without being given away either.

    ladder holds
    80
    l1_reveals_proof
    12
    single_line_proof
    16

    Not repairable — a lemma name that is the proof is true information about the problem, not a defect to hide. Both flags ride in the hint_caveat column so a hint-strength comparison can hold these rows out instead of averaging the ladder's collapse into its success.

    The rows overlap, so the flags do not sum. What survives is a clean-ladder set of 80 seeds on which levels 1 → 2 → 3 can honestly be read as increasing help — and 20 where the claim would not hold, named rather than dropped.

    The goal state is Lean's own error message

    An environment that shows a prover its goal state has to get that state from somewhere. The obvious route — close the prefix with sorry and ask what remains — is the one that bit us: a proof that is merely unfinished then looks the same as a proof that is finished, and partial work gets scored as progress it did not make.

    So the environment never closes anything. It assembles the tactics played so far with no closing body and calls Lean once. Lean's complaint is the observation:

    flowchart LR
  A["tactics so far
    (no closing body)"] --> L["one Lean call"]
  L -->|"any other error"| R["rejected
    state unchanged"]
  L -->|"'unsolved goals'"| K["accepted — the error body
    is the goal state"]
  L -->|"elaborates clean"| S["solved"]
  classDef n fill:#e2f0ef,stroke:#0E7C7B,color:#12312f
  classDef g fill:#d7ece4,stroke:#0E7C7B,color:#12312f
  class A,L,R,K n
  class S g

    Nothing is reconstructed and nothing is inferred. What the solver reads is what Lean printed. Two further locks close the usual escapes: set_option autoImplicit false goes into every header, so a misspelled identifier cannot be quietly absorbed as a fresh implicit binder; and a pass requires no errors, no sorries, and no uses sorry or failed warning — with the seeds' axiom closure already restricted to propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

    Two provers, two clocks

    A tactic prover and a whole-proof prover cannot share an episode. BFS-Prover reads a goal state and answers with one line; Goedel-Prover is handed theorem … := by sorry and answers with the whole proof. Asking either to work the other's way measures the mismatch, not the model.

    flowchart TB
  subgraph T["tactic prover — one line per action"]
    G1["goal state"] --> S1["sample 16 tactics"]
    S1 --> V1["Lean accepts one"]
    V1 --> G1
  end
  subgraph W["whole-proof prover — one proof per attempt"]
    P1["statement"] --> A1["write entire proof"]
    A1 --> V2["Lean reports diagnostics"]
    V2 --> A1
  end
  T -. "same token budget" .- W
  classDef n fill:#e2f0ef,stroke:#0E7C7B,color:#12312f
  class G1,S1,V1,P1,A1,V2 n

    Budget is what makes them comparable. Counting actions flatters the whole-proof model absurdly — one action for an entire proof against forty for a search — and counting attempts flatters the other. Both spend generated tokens, so tokens are the currency. Measuring it corrected our own guess: we assumed the tactic search was the expensive one, and it turned out to solve in a median 894 tokens against 8192 for the whole-proof loop.

    What a palette can and cannot repair

    Both provers fail with the same Lean message — Unknown constant — for two different reasons. Either the model reached for a lemma it could not name, or it was handed the name and copied it wrong. Only the first is a knowledge gap, and only the first is something an environment can supply.

    A gap the palette closes

    Artin_exercise_2_11_3 baseline Unknown identifier `exists_orderOf_eq_card_eq_two` palette 0/3 → 2/3

    The model knew a lemma existed and guessed its name. Supplying the name fixed it.

    A gap it cannot

    mathd_algebra_208 offered Real.sqrt_eq_iff_eq_sq wrote Real.sqrt_eq_iff_sq_eq every arm 0/3

    Two characters transposed, repeated across four revisions while Lean named the error each time. Even the arm that hands over the finished proof does not rescue it.

    Those two cards were 8 seeds — enough to name a mechanism, not to size it. Running the classifier over all 1,200 control episodes sized it, and the answer was not the one the anecdotes suggested:

    model · arm not in palette miscopied invented
    bfs · closed 49426 10
    bfs · open 45521 29
    goedel · closed 1959 0
    goedel · open 865 3
    share 92% 4.5% 3%

    Miscopying is 4.5%, not the 26–52% the small sample showed. And a third category had been hiding inside “knowledge gap”: names invented by extending a real one along Mathlib’s naming grammar — exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card becomes …_card_of_dvd. Those rise when a palette is offered (10 → 29 for the tactic prover): showing names supplies the pattern for making up more.

    Why the palette could not have worked

    92% of unknown-constant errors name something we never offered. That is not a delivery problem, so no amount of moving the list closer to the generation point would repair it. The cause is upstream, and short problems make it visible.

    6.9distinct passing proofs per short seed
    21of 23 solved two or more ways
    96%names in winning proofs, outside the palette
    11names inside it

    A theorem has many proofs. Our palette is extracted from one of them — the seed’s own verified proof — so it aims at a single route out of roughly seven. Axler_exercise_1_3 offers three names; the proofs that actually succeeded used add_assoc, add_comm, add_left_comm, add_right_inj, Module.End. Not one overlap.

    This is why the open-book arm was flat in all four McNemar tests (p ≥ 0.28). The aid was not weak; it was aimed elsewhere. A palette built from a single proof cannot help a prover that is free to take a different one — so the repair is to rebuild it around the statement’s concepts, not to find a better delivery channel.

    What the demo is showing you

    The highlighted goal is what the prover actually sees

    The reference implementation prompts one goal with its case header stripped. We were concatenating every open goal, headers included — a shape the model never saw in training. That is the tinted block.

    A rejected tactic costs nothing

    State is unchanged on failure, so the solver adapts in place; Rollback returns to any earlier verified state. Palette cards are extracted from the row’s own verified proof and validated by #check — the environment never invents docs.

    Control: three provers, 100 certified seeds

    Every cell is 300 episodes — 100 seeds × 3 independent plays. Benchmarks stay separated because they behave differently, and the gap between them (28% against 60% for BFS) is larger than any effect measured against it.

    ProverInterfaceProofNetminiF2F
    BFS-Prover-V2-7Bone tactic per action · 8,192 tok14/5030/50
    Goedel-Prover-V2-8Bwhole proof + diagnostics · 8,192 tok12/5030/50
    gpt-5.6-lunahosted · no budget · ceiling reference50/5050/50

    All three controls ran at their model's declared budget. The BFS control was re-measured to make that true: an earlier run at 16,384 tokens and 200 actions gave 60.0 and 28.0, against 58.0 and 28.0 at the declared 8,192 and 40. Halving the token budget and cutting the action ceiling fivefold cost that prover nothing on the seeds. What the re-measurement buys is a comparable environment-limit rate — under the same ceiling, 8.0% of treatment episodes end with the search still progressing against 5.0% of control episodes, a hardness signal independent of Pass@3 that the earlier budget mismatch had made unreadable.

    Are the bred rows harder?

    Both arms, 307 treatment rows against the 100-seed control. Drop is control minus treatment in percentage points; intervals are 95% bootstrap over row indices. Benchmarks are never pooled — the control is balanced 50/50 and the treatment is 169/138.

    Every drop is positive and only one interval excludes zero. That one is Goedel-Prover-V2 on ProofNet: 24.0% against 6.5%, a drop of 17.5pp. The others point the same way and cannot be separated from zero at this sample size — the control has 50 rows per benchmark, which bounds the resolution of every comparison drawn against it. That is a property of the control set, not evidence the remaining drops are absent, and a larger control is the first thing that would buy more.

    Can a model prove a row whose every ingredient it can already prove?

    The drops above ask whether bred rows are harder. This asks something they cannot. Every released row records a parent chain, and all 307 resolve to control seeds with no broken ancestor — so for each row we can take the seeds its lineage reaches, keep only the rows whose every seed the model solves at Pass@3, and ask how often it still misses the child. Conditioning that way is what separates this from a difficulty measure: a model cannot register a gap on a lineage it could not prove in the first place, so low capability cannot inflate the number.

    ModelBenchQFailgap95% CIrescue
    BFS-V2-7BProofNet674567.2%[55.3, 77.2]15/102
    miniF2F1034543.7%[34.5, 53.3]10/35
    Goedel-V2-8BProofNet443886.4%[73.3, 93.6]5/125
    miniF2F1064643.4%[34.4, 52.9]11/32
    gpt-5.6-lunaProofNet16910.6%[0.1, 3.3]—
    miniF2F13800.0%[0.0, 2.7]—

    Both open-weight provers fail a large share of children whose every root they can prove — 67.2% and 86.4% on ProofNet, 43.7% and 43.4% on miniF2F. The hosted model fails 1 of 307, and that near-zero floor is what makes the others readable: the gap is not an artifact of the harness, because a model exists that does not have it. Rescue is the complement — a root seed missed and the child solved anyway. Q is model-dependent by construction: a model that solves fewer seeds conditions on fewer lineages, which is why Goedel's ProofNet denominator (44) is smaller than BFS's (67).

    The ceiling model answers a question about us

    An episodic harness with a strict success test invites one objection: maybe the scores measure the environment, not the provers. A verifier that were too strict, an extractor that mis-read replies, a budget set too tight — all would depress every model at once, and a low number would say nothing about mathematics.

    100of 100 seeds solved by gpt-5.6-luna
    91solved on the first attempt alone
    0seeds that resisted it
    300episodes, same environment as the rest

    An environment that fabricated failures could not admit a perfect score. Statement handling, the step rule, proof-body splicing and the completeness test do not stand between a capable prover and a proof.

    The claim is narrow on purpose. What this validates is the part the hosted model shares with the others — environment, verifier, success test. It says nothing about the 8,192-token budget, which that interface cannot enforce. The budget is defended separately: it is identical on both sides of every drop we report.

    The same number reads a second way. A frontier model saturates both benchmarks completely while two dedicated prover checkpoints solve a quarter to three fifths of the same problems. ProofNet and miniF2F no longer separate the strongest models from each other. That is the gap the treatment set exists to reopen.

    It does not reopen the gap for the frontier model

    On the 307 treatment rows gpt-5.6-luna solves 306 at Pass@3 — 168/169 on ProofNet and 138/138 on miniF2F — against 100/100 on the seeds. The single failure is one doubly-mutated group-theory row. Whatever the generated problems do to the local checkpoints, they do not restore a measurable gap at the frontier, and that is reported rather than the result the construction was aimed at.

    Two readings are available and this data does not separate them. The treatment rows may genuinely not be harder for a model of that capability; or the ceiling may be too close for the difference to show, since a model at 100/100 on the control has almost no room to fall. What the number does establish is the direction of the claim the corpus can support — it separates dedicated prover checkpoints from each other and from the frontier, and it is not evidence about frontier-model difficulty.

    Prefill: an interface fix that is not a capability gain

    Goedel's official template asks for a prose proof plan before any Lean. Without a budget that is harmless; under one it is not. Failing attempts spent a median 4,096 tokens — the entire window — on analysis, against 1,458 for attempts that proved the theorem. So we open its turn with ```lean4 / import Mathlib and let it continue a code block rather than choose how to start.

    pass@3 — unchanged

    closed · ProofNet

    closed · miniF2F
    28→30
    open · ProofNet
    15→16
    open · miniF2F
    26→31

    Four paired McNemar tests, all null: p = 1.000, 0.688, 1.000, 0.180.

    wasted attempts — collapses

    closed · before

    15%
    open · before
    52%

    Share of attempts producing no checkable Lean. Median tokens per attempt: 3,949 → 719.

    The prefill changes what the harness measures, not what the model can prove. Attempts that burned the window on prose were attempts that were going to fail; removing the prose makes them fail sooner and six times more cheaply. We adopt it for the cost and keep the un-prefilled 600 episodes so the choice stays auditable.

    The release, and how it was checked

    535 generated theorems with complete Lean proofs. Every one carries the reasoning behind each judgement it received, including the passes that disagreed, and the result of every mechanical check. The rows that did not make it are here too, with their reasons, because a corpus that shows only its survivors cannot be checked.

    What it is made of

    Topic is a property of the seed, so it is read through the lineage: each row's roots are taken from its identifier and each root's topic from the seed sheet. Set against the seed donuts on Seeds, these say what the corpus grew into on the axis it was bred from.

    ProofNet lineage

    miniF2F lineage

    What was thrown away

    1226 certified rows were considered. Admission required strong from two independent passes of the judge.

    How a row got here

    Each gate, and what kind of thing settles it. Lean decides the questions that have an answer; a model is asked only the questions that do not. Coverage is uneven and the table says so — some checks were switched on partway through these campaigns, and a row without a check is not a row that failed it.

    How much a verdict is worth

    The judge was run twice over all 1233 rows — same inputs, same order, no shared state — so that its disagreement with itself could be measured rather than assumed. It is why no single verdict decides a row here.

      Open decisions

      1 · Corpus scale settled

      ~250 accepted rows per benchmark, miniF2F and ProofNet only. PutnamBench is out of the experiment — six seeds and thirteen rows cannot carry statistics, and its seeds are the hardest in the pool.

      • 239 rows carry over from EML-1; roughly half the target already exists
      • New seeds: 80–100 per benchmark, taking coverage from 4% of the pool to about 20%
      • No per-seed cap — breadth comes from more seeds, not from rationing children

      2 · Shape: wide, selectively deep settled

      EML-1 was 19–20 seeds carrying six children each, with one seed producing 29 rows. Human novelty QA rejected 86–95% of what survived certification, mostly as restatement and near-duplication — which is what breeding six siblings from one ancestor produces.

      • Breadth layer: generations 1–2 across every new seed
      • Depth layer: 12–15 seeds only, carried to generation 5–10, chosen after the breadth pass
      • The depth layer is what the lineage transfer experiment needs; the breadth layer is what the diversity criticism needs

      3 · Seeds for ProofNet settled

      Switch to the audited corrected release. All 367 ship a verified proof, so Gen-0 proof completion — the reason ProofNet seeds were never widened — costs nothing. The released set's flagged ancestry becomes a stated limitation rather than a growing one.

      4 · Serving stack

      • llama.cpp locally — logprobs work, reproduces the reference ordering
      • Cloud GPU + vLLM — exact reproduction, real cost, makes a wide run feasible

      Recommend llama.cpp for ablations; decide on vLLM once 18-seed timings are known.

      5 · Model split settled

      Generation and verification now run on different models, so nothing grades a sibling of its own output.

      • Generator: gpt-5.6-luna — statement and proof
      • Verifier: gpt-5.6-sol — statement/Lean alignment, and the informalizer role
      • Judge stays on the generator model, crossing it against the informalizer

      This closes two recorded limitations at once, and re-running the 357-item benchmark under the split adds an ablation row.

      6 · Budget to measure

      At the current 2.75% end-to-end yield, 260 new rows need ~9,500 slots; at a 5.5% yield they need ~4,700. Which one we are at is the thing a 200-slot pilot settles before the wide run is committed.
